summary: This best current practice examines the use of Source-Specific Multicast across peering points between networks in specified deployment scenarios. It describes the setup process for multicast delivery across administrative domains and the functions needed to support it.

eli5.summary: When two networks want to share a live broadcast, they have to agree on how to hand it over. This describes how.

subtitle: How two networks hand live multicast traffic to each other: five peering setups and the guidelines around them.

tldr.problem: Multicast saves bandwidth for live video and large downloads, but content often has to cross from one administrative domain to another over a peering point, and the two operators have to agree on many technical and operational details.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC covers Source-Specific Multicast with PIM-SSM and BGP across the peering point in five use cases (native multicast, a GRE tunnel, or Automatic Multicast Tunneling), and lists the information the two domains must exchange.
tldr.outcome: It gives operators a checklist for provisioning, routing, bandwidth, logging, troubleshooting, security and privacy. It is a Best Current Practice and nothing in the metadata obsoletes it.

today: RFC 8313 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 213). The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its AMT tunnel technology is defined in RFC 7450.

sections.title: Goals and Scope
sections.content:
Content such as live video streaming and software downloads suits multicast delivery, which can save significant resources in any given administrative domain. When the content has to cross domains, it passes through an inter-domain peering point. This RFC has two objectives: describe the technical process and guidelines for setting up multicast delivery across peering points through a set of use cases, and catalog all the information the domains must exchange to support it.

The scenario is that Administrative Domain 1 (AD-1) sources content to end users (EUs) in Administrative Domain 2 (AD-2). AD-1 is native multicast enabled. The peering point is assumed to be a private peering point between just the two domains, except where the broadcast case of an Internet Exchange Point is discussed.

The RFC recommends that only Source-Specific Multicast (SSM) be used between domains, because the source address of the stream (S,G) is known. It assumes PIM-SSM and BGP across the peering point, plus AMT and/or GRE depending on the scenario. Any-Source Multicast peering is out of scope, as are end users originating content, transit-provider setups, and billing settlements.
sections.eli5: Two TV companies want to share one broadcast instead of sending a separate copy to every house. The paper explains how they can hand it over safely and who does what.

sections.title: The Five Peering Use Cases
sections.content:
A client in AD-2 learns the (S,G) pair, meaning the source and the group (stream) identifier, and joins that stream. How the stream crosses the peering point depends on which parts of the path support multicast.

  • 3.1 Native multicast: both domains and the peering point are multicast enabled. This is the most efficient use of bandwidth. The drawback is that AD-1 cannot count end users or bytes delivered, so that data has to be collected by the application layer.
  • 3.2 GRE tunnel: the peering point is not multicast enabled, so a GRE tunnel (RFC 2784) between border routers carries the multicast protocols. It supports partial deployments but needs manual configuration and must be established before the stream starts. The tunnel server should advertise routes only to the application sources.
  • 3.3 AMT, both domains multicast enabled: an AMT relay in AD-1 and an AMT gateway in AD-2 form a tunnel dynamically across the peering point.
  • 3.4 AMT, AD-2 not multicast enabled: each end-user device runs a gateway and builds its own AMT tunnel to a relay in AD-1. This is equivalent to unicast delivery through AD-2. The number of tunnels equals the number of users, but each tunnel can count its user and the bytes delivered.
  • 3.5 Multiple AMT tunnels through AD-2: AD-2 places AMT nodes (a gateway and a relay together) at the peering point and at its edge. A single tunnel crosses the peering point, which relieves the traffic load of Use Case 3.4. No change is needed in AD-1.

For the AMT cases, finding the right relay for each (S,G) is still described as subject to ongoing work.
sections.eli5: There are five ways to pass the broadcast along. Sometimes the road is already built for it, and sometimes you have to dig a private tunnel to carry it through.

sections.title: Bandwidth and Congestion Control
sections.content:
Multicast carried across non-controlled networks must follow congestion control principles, as unicast does. A non-controlled network is one with no bandwidth policy beyond best effort with a fair share under congestion. Many multicast deployments start inside one domain with reserved bandwidth and no congestion control, so the issue needs specific attention when moving to inter-domain peering.

Both domains must agree on a consistent traffic-management policy. If AD-1 sends traffic that does not adapt to congestion and AD-2 carries it as best effort, drops under congestion leave undecodable packets that clog AD-2 while competing traffic loses its fair share. The RFC notes this is a transport or application issue, not a multicast technology issue.

AMT tunnels that end at the user device scale with the number of users, not with the amount of content, and can create a very large amount of replicated traffic near the relay. The RFC therefore recommends rate adaptation even inside controlled networks in that case. Rate adaptation here means that users who see congestion join a lower-bitrate (S,G) stream, which also makes group membership change more often.
sections.eli5: If a pipe is too small and someone keeps pouring in more water than it can carry, everything gets messy. Everyone has to agree to pour less when the pipe is full.

sections.title: Routing and Relay Discovery
sections.content:
The routing goal is that the user receives the stream from the most optimal source, which maximizes the multicast part of the path and minimizes the unicast part and the overall distance.

For native multicast, the two domains advertise the source addresses over the peering points, exchange information such as capacity and utilization, and run compatible multicast protocols. A GRE tunnel needs the same process.

AMT is more complex because two goals must be met: find the closest relay that has multicast connectivity to the source, and keep the unicast tunnel short. An AMT relay receives the multicast natively and encapsulates it in unicast toward gateways. An AMT gateway sits on the endpoint and passes join and leave requests from the application. As an illustration (the RFC says the method is up to operators), a gateway can use a DNS query to get an anycast relay address, contact the nearest relay, and receive the relay's own unicast address. It then does a three-way handshake and gives the relay the (S,G) so the relay can join the stream.

On a broadcast peering point such as an IXP, several upstream domains may forward the same (S,G), and PIM assert makes only one forward it. A downstream domain may then receive traffic from a provider it has no agreement with. The RFC lists three options: tunnel across the LAN (a GRE tunnel between the actual border routers is specifically recommended), have only one upstream domain source multicast, or have federated upstream domains agree on a consistent policy.
sections.eli5: Your device asks, who is the nearest helper that can get me this show? A helper answers, they set up a private line, and the show flows down it.

sections.title: Provisioning, Logs, Monitoring and Troubleshooting
sections.content:
The RFC lists what the two domains must set up and share. For provisioning, they need enough capacity for multicast delivery and for back-office connections, and AD-2 must deliver the metadata that tells the user how to get the multicast stream and any unicast fallback. Where AMT is used, the user needs an AMT client, AD-2 relays need the allowed source and group addresses, and DNS must help a gateway find the best relay.

For authentication, a unique identifier is recommended for each master account, and AD-2 is expected to set up accounts for use by AD-1. AD-1 is the one that escalates problems, because customers contact the content source, which is part of AD-1.

For logs, AD-1 takes primary responsibility for customer experience. Useful logs from AD-2 include aggregate usage and failure information, security logs, and on-demand access, application and syslog data. Multicast gives the source less visibility than unicast, because the stream is per user only after the last replication, which is usually not in AD-1.

For monitoring and troubleshooting, both domains monitor performance, agree on probes, and tell each other when problems appear. Users complain to the source provider, which passes complaints to AD-1. AD-1 then works out whether the cause is in its own network or in AD-2 and sends AD-2 details such as the kind of problem, when it started and the affected address blocks. Diagnostics can use tools such as traceroute and mtrace, but AMT does not allow the passing of traceroute or mtrace requests, so troubleshooting with AMT usually needs direct work on the devices.
sections.eli5: Both companies keep notebooks about how the show is going, and they agree to call each other when something breaks and share what they see so they can fix it together.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
SSM multicast is described as self-protecting against illicit sources, because forwarding requires an (S,G) membership report from a receiver and reverse path forwarding is part of the protocols. Receivers can still attack it in two ways. First, they can create large numbers of (S,G) states, which loads the control plane. This is mitigated by defining the permissible (S,G) set, for example with access control lists on last-hop routers, which means AD-1 must tell AD-2 its valid (S,G) pairs. Second, a receiver can join so much valid content that it congests shared links. The mitigation is policing the traffic per end user at the point of last replication, for example by limiting the number of joined (S,G)s per user.

On content security, the model assumed is end-to-end: confidentiality, DRM, and user authentication and authorization are handled by the source provider and the receiving application. With plain multicast, AD-2 does not know which user is authenticated for which content, so an unauthenticated user could obtain a copy of the encrypted stream. The short-term recommendation is to isolate the source and group addresses for different content bundles, tell AD-2 the (S,G) patterns, and let AD-2 use its existing per-user mechanisms to filter them.

Encryption at the peering point may be used by agreement, and is recommended for tunnels across transit domains. Operational data such as logs should by default be exchanged over authenticated, encrypted channels, and the two domains are expected to have a plan to shut down the peering point and move multicast to alternative peering points after a security breach.
sections.eli5: A sneaky viewer might ask for far too many shows and clog the pipes, or try to copy a locked show. So the networks check who is allowed to ask for what, and send their notes in sealed envelopes.

sections.title: Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
AD-1 operates on behalf of the content source, so privacy between the user and AD-1 is generally the same as without multicast. AD-2 is not required to learn more about user behavior than it already would, unless AD-1 and AD-2 agree on it and the user approves.

The one multicast-specific concern is that AD-2 can know or reconstruct what content a user is consuming, because it sees which users join which (S,G) streams. The RFC says privacy against AD-2 is lower than with unicast, even in Use Case 3.4, because AMT has no transport-layer encryption. It suggests end-to-end encryption and future work such as DTLS between the AMT relay and the user.

The source operator, on the other hand, does not natively know which user consumes which content when AD-2 does the replication. The model only protects against exposure to intermediate parties such as AD-2.
sections.eli5: The network in the middle might be able to guess which shows you watch by seeing who asks for what. Locking the show helps, but it cannot hide everything.
